summary: RFC 6567 describes the motivation and use cases for carrying ISDN user-to-user information across SIP. As networks move to SIP, this document defines how to interwork the ISDN DSS1 user-user information element with SIP so the data survives the translation.

eli5.summary: Old phone lines and new internet phone systems speak different languages. This document explains how to pass a small attached message from one to the other without it getting lost.

questions: how does sip interwork with isdn user-to-user
what is the isdn uui size limit
subtitle: How to carry ISDN user-to-user signalling data across SIP using the isdn-uui package and the User-to-User header.

tldr.problem: Call centers rely on the ISDN User-to-User service, and as networks move to SIP that data must keep flowing between ISDN and SIP endpoints.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7434 defines the isdn-uui package for the User-to-User header field of RFC 7433, with a protocol discriminator octet, hex encoding, a 128 octet limit and rules for UACs, UASs and gateways.
tldr.outcome: SIP endpoints and ISDN gateways can exchange UUS1 implicit data, and data too long for ISDN is silently dropped at the gateway while the call proceeds.

today: RFC 7434 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2015, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7433.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 7434 describes a usage of the User-to-User header field from RFC 7433 to carry UUI in ISDN interworking scenarios. It covers three call-control items: the Q.931 DSS1 User-user information element, the Q.957.1 DSS1 User-to-User Signalling (UUS) supplementary service, and the Q.763 User-to-User information parameter. Public and private ISDN, including QSIG, are both addressed.

The usage is not limited to interworking. It describes a usage where interworking is possible, and it can also be used directly between two SIP terminals. The package is identified by the value isdn-uui of the purpose parameter. The motivation and use cases are in RFC 6567.
sections.eli5: This document teaches the internet phone system how to carry the little sticky notes that old phone lines allow on calls.

sections.title: The ISDN User-to-User Service
sections.content:
ISDN has a user signalling bearer service and a User-to-User Signalling supplementary service, both of which carry data in the signalling channel. There are three UUS variants. UUS1 exchanges data during call setup and clearing, and comes in implicit and explicit forms. UUS2 exchanges it between ALERTING and CONNECT. UUS3 exchanges it while the call is Active. The service is always requested by the calling user.

This document defines only UUS1 implicit, the most widely deployed variant and the one matching the requirements in RFC 6567. In UUS1 implicit, the presence of the data itself is the request. The QSIG private network specifications define no UUS1 implicit service, but the RFC says evidence suggests some vendors built one proprietarily, so the package can be used with it on the same assumptions.

The service carries a maximum of 128 octets of user information plus a one-octet protocol discriminator, only one piece of UUI per message, and has no encryption or integrity protection. Some early ISDN implementations had a limit of 32 octets, which are understood not to be deployed now.

Some ISDN features interact with SIP. Call transfer cancels ISDN User-to-User services, so UUI cannot be exchanged in transactions clearing down the SIP dialog after a transfer. UUS1 implicit is not possible with SIP conferencing. With diversion, UUS1 data is sent to the forwarded-to user.
sections.eli5: The old phone system lets you attach a short note, up to about 128 bytes, when you start a call. This document copies that exact rule for internet phones.

sections.title: Relation to SIP-T
sections.content:
One option is SIP-T (RFC 3372), which carries the whole ISUP or QSIG message as a MIME body end to end. That is reasonable when SIP-T encapsulation is already used. For true ISDN interworking, though, it would force an implementer to understand many elements of ISUP syntax just to read one piece of data.

The RFC therefore prefers interworking the data through the native SIP mechanism, the User-to-User header field.
sections.eli5: You could mail the whole phone-company letter just to deliver one note. It is simpler to copy the note onto a SIP envelope.

sections.title: Transition Away from ISDN
sections.content:
The package will likely start with one UA acting as an ISDN gateway and the other a native SIP endpoint. As networks move off ISDN, both ends may become native SIP, and there is an opportunity to move to a more general usage of RFC 7433.

During the move, an endpoint can carry the UUI both as ISDN and as a future enhanced package, in the same or different messages. A receiving ISDN gateway uses the ISDN package, and a native SIP endpoint uses the new one.
sections.eli5: While the world switches phone systems, you can write the note in both the old style and the new style, and each reader picks the one they understand.

sections.title: UAC and UAS Requirements
sections.content:
Both UACs and UASs MUST meet RFC 7433 and may use this package only with the initial INVITE and the BYE of an INVITE dialog. Other methods, re-INVITEs and other dialogs are precluded.

A UAC that wants to send or allow UUI MUST put a User-to-User header field in the initial INVITE, even when the only content is the protocol discriminator octet, because that header is the implicit request for the service. It SHOULD set purpose to isdn-uui, though omitting it is permitted for earlier implementations. A UAC or UAS MUST NOT include more than one such header field per request or response, and MUST NOT send it in a dialog whose original INVITE did not include it. A UAS MAY include it in responses to the initial INVITE and in BYE messages only if the INVITE carried it.

If a receiver gets multiple such header fields, it MUST discard all of them, since there is no way to tell which is intended. A redirect server MUST NOT include the header in the header URI parameter of a 3xx response. The 128 octet limit applies before hex encoding or after decoding. The value isdn-interwork from earlier drafts is implemented by some vendors, and implementations could find it useful to parse it like isdn-uui.
sections.eli5: The first message of the call must hold up a hand to say a note is coming. After that, only one note per message, and if two notes show up, both are thrown away.

sections.title: UUI Contents and Coding
sections.content:
The only content defined for the package is isdn-uui, and the only encoding is hex. A sender MAY include the matching content and encoding parameters but need not. A receiver MUST ignore the header field if either parameter has a different value.

The first octet of the UUI data MUST be a protocol discriminator following Table 4-26 of Q.931. The receiving application decides what to do with it. It is needed at gateways to map into the ISDN fields. Valid values come from the ITU-T and there is no IANA registry for them.

Section 11 adds isdn-uui as a value for both purpose and content in the ABNF of RFC 7433, and Section 12 defines the media feature tag sip.uui-isdn.
sections.eli5: The first byte of the note is a label saying what kind of note it is. The rest is up to the people sending it.

sections.title: ISDN Interworking Gateways
sections.content:
Gateways MUST support the UAS and UAC requirements and MUST support only the isdn-uui package on interworked dialogs. They take octet-structured data from the ISDN side and encode it as hex for the User-to-User header field, and decode in the reverse direction. They treat all content as binary and do not check the protocol discriminator.

Responsibility for the limits sits with the end UA. If data is too long for the ISDN, the gateway discards the UUI data but still interworks the request, with no notice to the sender. Because the data would then be missing from the ISDN SETUP message, the service is unavailable for the remainder of the call under UUS1 implicit.

The uui option tag is not interworked at a gateway, and a gateway MUST NOT treat its omission as a reason to skip interworking. A Require: uui will make the request fail at a UAS or gateway that lacks support.
sections.eli5: A translator at the border copies the note. If the note is too long for the old system, the translator quietly leaves it behind, so keep notes short.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document adds no security requirements beyond RFC 7433. Because it interworks with ISDN, the general security considerations of SIP to ISUP interworking in RFC 3398 apply, and a gateway should not blindly trust ISUP from the PSTN.

The ISDN service may be less secure than SIP. Its security exists hop by hop, not end to end, and varies from high in some places to low in others. Data that is private or needs guaranteed authenticity may be unsuitable for this package, and a different package or data transfer method may be needed.
sections.eli5: The old phone system checks notes at each handoff, not the whole way, so do not put secrets on them.
